beats.narration: This week, Google DeepMind shows a world model you can steer in real time.
Researchers test whether a frontier AI model can really run a robot, and where it fails.

visual.credit: SenseNova et al. · ZAP project page (Luma AI)

beats.narration: Plus a startup whose robots learn from one demonstration, Toyota building robotaxis for Waymo, and self-driving excavators.

visual.credit: Machenta · Toyota · Bedrock Robotics via TechCrunch

beats.narration: This is Pixels to Actions. Every week, we go through what's new in robotics and physical AI.

visual.sub: Every week: what's new in robotics and physical AI

segments.label: NEWS
segments.headline: Genie 4: a world you can steer

beats.narration: Story one. Google DeepMind announced Genie 4, its new world model.
A world model is an AI that generates a world as you move through it.
Think of a video game with no game engine. The AI itself draws what happens next.
You set an event in motion, and Genie 4 simulates what happens next.
DeepMind says that includes how the world responds, how it sounds, and how the people in it move.
In DeepMind's recordings, people steer with keyboard controls, and use text prompts to change the scene as it evolves.
You can type a change, like new weather, a camera move, or a new person or object,
and Gemini adapts your prompt to fit the scene.
It's also DeepMind's first real-time world model to generate audio natively:
the sound is made by Genie 4 itself.
So why is this on a robotics channel?
DeepMind says Genie 4 can help with developing training environments for robots and agents.
Like a flight simulator, but for robots: a safe place to practice, in endless variations.

left.title: Flight simulator
left.sub: Pilots practice before the real thing

right.title: World model
right.sub: Robots could practice in generated worlds

beats.narration: DeepMind's stated aim is to test how AI systems navigate different environments
before bringing them to the real world.

visual.sub: then the real world

beats.narration: To keep a simulation on task, DeepMind puts a second AI in the loop:

visual.text: A second AI in the loop

beats.narration: Gemini three point eight Flash.
As Genie draws the world, Gemini watches the scene, breaks the goal into steps, and checks each new frame to verify that the step succeeded.

steps.label: Watch
steps.sub: the scene as Genie draws it

steps.label: Break into steps
steps.sub: the goal, one step at a time

steps.label: Check
steps.sub: each new frame: did the step work?

beats.narration: Think of a director calling out each next move while the scene is being filmed.

visual.sub: Gemini plans the steps · Genie 4 draws them

beats.narration: On the announcement page, a simulated robot arm holds a pipette and dispenses liquid into a lab plate.
DeepMind's Gemini 4 Argon also works with Genie 4
to simulate Apptronik's Apollo humanoid playing checkers.
Here's how. Argon breaks the task into steps, and feeds each step to Genie 4 as a text caption while the simulation renders.
Because those captions steer the scene as it goes,
DeepMind says the simulation can adapt as it moves toward finishing the task.
Why it matters. DeepMind pitches world models as safe training grounds for robots, and it's already experimenting with Genie 4 alongside its Gemini Robotics work.
Reality check. Those robot clips are generated simulations. DeepMind doesn't say any robot was trained in Genie 4, and it gives no benchmark numbers.

items.text: No robot reported trained in it

beats.narration: DeepMind also says visual details and object permanence
things staying where they should, can still drift over time.

visual.sub: things staying where they should

beats.narration: It lists complex physical interactions and spatial accuracy among the areas it's still researching.
For now, it's a research preview for trusted testers.

segments.label: PAPER
segments.headline: Can GPT-6 Astra run a real robot?

beats.narration: Story two. Frontier AI models, like one called GPT-6 Astra,
can now directly control robots.
Frontier means among the largest, most capable AI models.

visual.sub: among the largest, most capable AI models

beats.narration: The ZAP paper describes GPT-6 Astra as a trillion-parameter model,
meaning about a trillion adjustable numbers inside it.

visual.sub: parameters: the adjustable numbers inside a model

beats.narration: Robots usually run on a different kind of model, a V-L-A: vision, language, action.
It sees camera images, reads an instruction, and outputs movements. It's trained on robot demonstrations.
GPT-6 Astra has no task- or robot-specific training. It reasons about the scene, and drives the robot through software.
But how well?
Here's the setup. The model sees camera images, works out a plan, and sends motion commands through a harness, a software layer that works like an interpreter for the robot.
First, a big report led by SenseNova, published earlier in October.
The report tested GPT-6 Astra on twelve benchmarks, which are standard test suites,
and on eight real robot platforms.
In simulation, it scored ninety-nine to one hundred percent on six benchmark suites,
but with help: it was allowed to learn in context from the benchmark's training set.
In plain terms: before testing, it studied example solutions,
and wrote itself a package of notes, motions and helper code, to look things up during the test.
It was also allowed up to ten times the usual number of steps. Think of an open-book exam, with extra time.

left.title: Open book
left.sub: Notes built from the training demos

right.title: Extra time
right.sub: Up to 10× the official step limit

beats.narration: On the real robots, there were no demonstrations and no notes package,
only context written by people, like joint limits and safety constraints.
An operator held an emergency stop,

visual.sub: held by a person on every real run

beats.narration: and success was judged from the physical result, not the model's own claim.
Simple pick-and-place, moving rigid objects, worked in seventeen of eighteen trials.
But plug insertion, which needs precise contact, went zero for eleven, across three robot platforms.
Why? The report says the model can tell a task is unfinished, but not which physical condition is unmet,
so its corrections don't converge. Looking done isn't the same as being done.
Like plugging in a charger in the dark: you can tell it isn't in, but not whether you're too high or too far left.

visual.sub: It can tell it's not in, not why

beats.narration: Real hardware adds its own limits. On one robot, two of three plug attempts ended with a joint collision fault.

items.label: PiPER plug attempts ended by a collision fault

beats.narration: Cloth folding and long mobile tasks were also markedly harder:
two of four folds, and nine of twenty-three navigation searches.
The authors' verdict: competent, but not yet practical.

visual.sub: SenseNova et al.: “not yet that of practical embodied intelligence”

beats.narration: Two new preprints, papers shared before peer review, try to close that gap.

visual.sub: LEXP · ZAP

beats.narration: The first, LEXP, doesn't retrain the model at all. The model's weights stay fixed. What changes is the information it's given before each move.
A planner splits the task into steps. After each attempt, LEXP writes down lessons from what actually happened, and when they apply, then feeds the relevant ones back.
Like a notebook of lessons the robot rereads before each move.

visual.sub: Same model, better notes

beats.narration: Across twelve real-world tasks, success rose from five point six percent for plain Astra, to sixty-three point nine percent.
That's twenty-three of thirty-six trials, against two of thirty-six for plain Astra.
With memory alone, just the history of its past attempts, it reached nineteen.

items.label: memory alone: history of past attempts

beats.narration: Those are the paper's own trials, on one two-armed robot, with three trials per task.
The second, ZAP from Luma AI, starts by splitting robot control into two skills: understanding what the task asks for, and knowing how to move.

left.title: What
left.sub: Understand the task and the scene

beats.narration: The authors tested a small open model, Qwen three point six.

visual.sub: a small open model

beats.narration: On its own, it succeeded in just sixteen point seven percent of real trials.
Looking closer, it understood the task, but only thirty-six percent of its motion calls were correct.
So ZAP teaches only the motion part, entirely in simulation,
on as few as forty deliberately simple tasks, with no real-world robot data.
The model practices, and learns from its own successful attempts. No bigger model teaches it.
Then it was tested on a real two-armed robot, on tasks it never trained on,
like handing a test tube between arms and placing it in a rack.
It succeeded on twenty-nine of thirty trials,
matching GPT-6 Astra in the same harness.
Cost matters too. In this harness, GPT-6 Astra takes three hundred ninety-seven seconds and four dollars eighty-seven cents per average real task.
The authors say ZAP matches it at three times the speed, and one seventeenth of the cost.
Why it matters. The ZAP authors argue that a small open model already understands robot tasks, and mainly lacks motion control. And that part, they show, can be taught in simulation.
Reality check. These are preprints with small trial counts, and precise contact, like plugging something in, was the weak spot.
LEXP lists its code as coming soon, and ZAP doesn't mention releasing code or weights.

items.text: ZAP: no code or weights mentioned

segments.label: NEWS
segments.headline: Robots that learn from one demo

beats.narration: Story three. A startup called Machenta came out of stealth,
saying its robots learn a new task from a single demonstration.
Founder Ed Johns announced a forty million dollar seed round, co-led by Creandum and USV.
Here's the usual way to teach a robot: collect demonstrations, then train the model on them, before you can use it.

left.title: The usual way
left.sub: Collect demos, train the model, then use it

right.title: Machenta's claim
right.sub: Show it once. No training, no waiting.

beats.narration: Machenta says robot models like VLAs are usually post-trained on many real demonstrations per task,
a process that can take days or weeks.

visual.sub: per task, says Machenta

beats.narration: Machenta's pitch is like showing a new coworker a task once.
Its model swaps the language part for a demonstration. Machenta calls it a V-D-A: vision, demo, action.
In its videos, a person demonstrates once, on objects the robot has never seen,
then rearranges them, steps back, and the robot does it alone, with no further training.
The company says the model was trained entirely in simulation,
without a single pixel of real-world training data.

visual.sub: in its training data, says Machenta

beats.narration: The idea is to use simulation to learn how to learn, not to memorize one task.

right.title: Learn to learn
right.sub: pick up new tasks from one demo

beats.narration: To do that, Machenta generates a vast range of random simulated tasks, objects and settings,
so the model has to work out what matters from whichever demonstration it's shown.
A common worry is the sim-to-real gap: a skill learned in a simulator breaks when reality differs.

visual.sub: Skills learned in simulation can break in reality

beats.narration: Machenta's answer: at test time, the demonstration and the camera images both come from the real world.
As it puts it, to the model, reality is just one more environment to adapt to.
Machenta says the same model runs on six different robots.
Here, three robots, each with a different gripper and camera setup,
work a line together in a one-person factory demo.
To stress-test it, Machenta ran tasks that reset themselves, for an hour each:
seventy-four of seventy-four block placements, seventy-eight of seventy-eight screwdriver handovers, and ninety-seven of ninety-nine attempts at standing a bottle upright.
Why it matters. Machenta claims one demonstration is enough to learn a new task.
Machenta argues that if every new task needs days or weeks of data and training,
robots stay too slow and too expensive to deploy at scale.

visual.sub: Machenta's argument for instant learning

beats.narration: Reality check. Machenta itself calls these tasks relatively simple.
And it says these results come from its first few months, mostly fundamental research.
The blog mentions no paper or code, and there's no independent evaluation yet.

segments.label: NEWS
segments.headline: Toyota will build robotaxis for Waymo

beats.narration: Story four. Toyota and Waymo announced the next phase of their self-driving partnership.
It builds on a preliminary agreement the two announced in April twenty twenty-five.
Toyota will build self-driving bZ4X cars for Waymo's driverless ride-hailing service.
The whole build happens under one roof, at Toyota's Takaoka plant in Japan, from assembling the base vehicle to integrating Waymo's self-driving hardware.
Think of a phone that leaves the factory with its key apps already installed.
That's straight from Toyota's release.
Testing and validation in Japan begin in twenty twenty-seven, with the United Kingdom and other Waymo markets planned for the following years.
Toyota's release spells out the timeline.
The two companies will also keep exploring self-driving technology for personally owned Toyota cars,
the kind people buy for themselves.

visual.sub: not only robotaxis

beats.narration: Why it matters. The companies say this will accelerate scaling safety-validated autonomous vehicles globally.
Toyota says it paves the way for Japan's first fully autonomous ride-hailing service
built on domestically manufactured vehicles.

visual.sub: domestically manufactured robotaxis

beats.narration: Reality check. Twenty twenty-seven is for testing and validation, not public rides. The release gives no fleet size, no city, and no date for paying passengers.

items.text: No fleet size or city given

beats.narration: Story five. Self-driving excavators just pulled in a very large funding round.
TechCrunch reports that Bedrock Robotics raised six hundred million dollars, at a valuation of four point one billion.
A Series C is a later funding round. The valuation is what the deal says the whole company is worth.

visual.sub: A later funding round · what the deal says the company is worth

beats.narration: TechCrunch notes it was founded in twenty twenty-four, and has raised nearly one billion dollars since.
The round was co-led by CapitalG and Emergence Capital.
Bedrock makes a self-driving kit that's retrofitted onto construction and other worksite vehicles.
Think of it as an add-on autopilot for machines that already exist.
Two months before the round, Bedrock moved its excavators beyond testing and pilots,
onto active construction sites.

visual.sub: two months before the round

beats.narration: Excavators with the kit are now working commercially, including at a Nevada water treatment facility,
a Texas earthwork site, and a civil sitework project with Zachry Construction.
Why excavators? According to Bedrock, it takes five years or more to master operating one,
and skilled operators are in short supply.
And a construction trade group, the Associated Builders and Contractors,
estimates that more than forty percent of construction workers will retire in the next five years.

items.label: of construction workers retiring within 5 years (ABC estimate)

beats.narration: The money is meant to speed up Bedrock's move to commercial work, at more construction sites.
Reality check. This comes from TechCrunch's report. It gives no count of machines deployed, and no revenue.
